item.title: NEVA: Natural-Language Co-Evolution and Validation of Microarchitectures
item.description: arXiv:2611.33346v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent large language model (LLM)-guided evolutionary approaches have demonstrated the potential to automate microarchitectural design exploration. However, existing approaches primarily evolve C++ simulator code rather than reasoning directly about the microarchitectural designs it represents. As C++ code embodies hardware designs with several layers of abstraction, evolving it directly forces LLMs to reason through implementation details rather than the actual architectural mechanisms, hardware state, and decision rules that define a microarchitectural design. To this end, we propose NEVA, an LLM-guided methodology that generates new microarchitectural policies by extracting, integrating and adapting architectural concepts from published research. NEVA extracts the underlying concepts from prior works into a structured knowledge library, which then guides the evolution of joint natural-language architectural specifications. This approach addresses three key challenges: architectural representation in natural language, validation of candidate designs under hardware constraints, and the coordination of microarchitecture components using diagnostic feedback through co-evolution. We evaluate NEVA across single-core and multicore configurations using SPEC CPU2017/2026, Google, GAP, and XSBench workloads, and compare specification-level evolution against code-level evolution across different search strategies. Under Claude Opus 5.5, NEVA discovers designs achieving up to 4.8% higher held-out single-core performance than the Pythia-Mockingjay baseline. A selected EvoX design achieves improvements of 3.4% and 1.5% under full and restricted memory bandwidth, respectively, although its multicore performance does not differ significantly from the baseline. The EvoX search evaluates 40 candidates over 2.2 days, with approximately $320 in LLM usage at API list prices.
item.dc:creator: Khoi Le, Sayanti Jana, Matthew DeLorenzo, Jeyavijayan Rajendran, Paul Gratz

item.title: WADJET: Whole-Job Authorization and Dispatch for Job Execution Trust on FPGA System-on-Chip Accelerators
item.description: arXiv:2611.33406v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: On an FPGA system-on-chip, the software that submits work to an accelerator also decides what the accelerator does. It writes the registers one by one, and the hardware runs whatever it finds, so faulty or compromised software can change one address or resend a job. Existing protections decide who may reach an accelerator or keep its data safe. Deciding whether one job was approved and is still unused takes three things in one place: the only way to the accelerator, the whole job held back until checked, and a record of used approvals. WADJET puts the three in one gate in FPGA logic. A separate authority encrypts and authenticates each approved job, with a sequence number, using Ascon-AEAD128. The gate verifies the whole job before releasing any part, accepts only a newer sequence number, uses it up, and writes the registers of an unmodified accelerator itself. The gate replaces only the processor's direct line to the registers and works beside the existing protections. In a software model, a check on each write ran jobs mixed from two approved ones; the whole-job rule released none. Its release path is proven on the Verilog for all inputs. On a Zynq-7020 running a language model, it released all 21,000 approved jobs and none of 14,700 altered or repeated ones. It needs a third of the lookup tables of ShEF's register protection, which protects more, and adds about ten microseconds to starting a job. It assumes trusted control of its key, reset, and configuration.
item.dc:creator: Mohamed El-Hadedy

item.title: From Entropy Source to Stochastic Bit-Stream: Low-Cost Converters for True-Random Stochastic Computing
item.description: arXiv:2611.33686v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Stochastic computing (SC) encodes values as the probability of ones in random bit-streams, which allows arithmetic circuits with very low area and power and a natural tolerance to faults. The accuracy and security of an SC system depend on the quality of those bit-streams. Conventional generators build them from pseudo-random or quasi-random sequences, which are predictable, periodic, and correlated across streams drawn from the same generator. This work proposes three methods for converting the unbiased outputs of a true random number generator (TRNG) into stochastic bit-streams (SBS) with arbitrary target probabilities: a block extraction and comparison circuit, a counter-logic circuit, and a cascaded majority-logic pipeline. All three accept bits from any true- random source and are built from standard CMOS logic. They reach the accuracy of a software random generator for both independent and correlated stream generation, and they support the common SC arithmetic operations with error that falls with stream length at the same rate. Hardware synthesis results show that the converters offer favorable area, energy, and area-delay trade-offs relative to pseudo- and quasi-random baselines. Under injected soft errors, block extraction degrades no faster than the best deterministic baseline. By bridging raw entropy sources and application-ready bit-streams, this work makes true-random SC practical on standard CMOS.
item.dc:creator: Mehran Moghadam, Abu Masum, M. Hassan Najafi, Sercan Aygun, Di Wu

item.title: L2C2: Enhancing Large-scale Chiplets for Agent Long-Context LLM Inference with Sparse and Distributed Attention
item.description: arXiv:2611.33691v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-context inference is a rising demand for LLMs, especially for agent applications. Sparse attention (SpAt) and chiplet technology are promising solutions to reduce computations and scale hardware performance. However, deploying SpAt on distributed chiplets necessitates context parallelism for workload partitioning, introducing complex distributed attention. In this work, we present L2C2, a system optimization for distributed SpAt in long-context inference. During the partial-prefill stage, we propose a novel Split-Comm Attention mechanism that leverages the high-bandwidth interconnect of chiplets to trade communication overhead for reduced memory access. We combine it with conventional Ring Attention to form a Bi-Mode method that adapts to varying input sequence lengths. During the decoding stage, we analyze the cause of memory access imbalance and address it by static interleaved token assignment. Dynamic agile cache balancing is also proposed to adapt to SpAt skewness. Evaluations show our optimization can achieve 1.45$\times$ and 1.53$\times$ speedup in partial-prefill and decoding with SpAt on large-scale chiplets.
item.dc:creator: Kangbo Bai, Zhonghua Mu, Hongze Zhou, Tianyu Jia

item.title: GPS: Guiding Phase-Level Prefetcher Selection with Data-Driven Method
item.description: arXiv:2611.33859v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hardware prefetching is a widely used technique for hiding off-chip memory latency. Modern processors increasingly adopt composite prefetchers that combine multiple prefetching engines to handle the diverse memory access patterns found in real applications. However, coordinating multiple prefetchers requires a policy selection algorithm that maps observed system feedback to appropriate prefetching policies. Existing approaches suffer from two key limitations. First, relying on only a small set of features can lead to misleading prefetcher policies due to incomplete visibility into the system state. Second, limited on-chip hardware resources force these designs to use simple mapping mechanisms that cannot effectively navigate the large prefetching policy space. To address these challenges, we propose GPS, a data-driven framework for prefetcher selection that leverages comprehensive profiling and offline learning. GPS collects a rich set of features that capture both system behaviors and hardware resource states, and uses an offline machine learning model to learn the mapping between these features and the IPC-best policy. By offloading complex policy generation to software, GPS eliminates the need for costly online exploration and enables lightweight runtime execution through pre-generated policy hints. GPS reduces the performance gap to only 2.6%, compared to 13.6% and 14.2% in prior state-of-the-art methods. We evaluate GPS on SPEC CPU2006, SPEC CPU2017, and GAP benchmark suites. GPS outperforms the state-of-the-art prefetcher selection method I-POP by 12.14%, 8.34%, and 14.17% in geometric-mean IPC, respectively. GPS achieves these gains with only 778 bits of additional on-chip storage for runtime policy control.
item.dc:creator: Buqing Xu, Mengming Li, Qijun Zhang, Ziyan Guo, Zhiyao Xie

item.title: MixMoMo: Accelerating Extra--Large MoE Inference with Mixed--Precision GPU--NPU Execution on Mobile Devices
item.description: arXiv:2611.33981v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mobile agents and on-device intelligence increasingly demand more capable models on smartphones. Through sparse expert activation, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) scales model capacity, yet growing numbers of fine-grained experts complicate loading and computation. Model compression complements expert offloading by reducing storage and computation costs. Among compression techniques, mixed-precision quantization assigns lower expert bitwidths to balance model quality and inference efficiency. However, existing offline metrics and routing scores fail to reflect expert quantization sensitivity, undermining precision assignment. Diverse bitwidths also complicate balanced expert allocation across GPUs and NPUs with distinct execution characteristics, while tile-wise dequantization underutilizes NPU vector parallelism. We present MixMoMo, an efficient mixed-precision inference runtime for extra-large MoE models on heterogeneous mobile SoCs. MixMoMo combines offline quantization-impact profiles with activation-based runtime risk estimates for quality-constrained expert bitwidth assignment. It further adopts precision-structured execution for balanced GPU-NPU expert allocation and HVX-parallel dequantization for efficient NPU vector utilization. Across three MoE models and five benchmarks on two mobile platforms, MixMoMo achieves average decoding speedups of 3.72x over uniform Q4_0 and 1.53x over the strongest mixed-precision MoE baseline.
item.dc:creator: Hailong Zou, Maoliang Li, Taohong Han, Haoze Chi, Zihao Zheng, Jiayu Chen, Xiang Chen

item.title: A Differential Computing Accelerator for LLM Inference Leveraging Bit-Slice Transition Sparsity
item.description: arXiv:2611.34630v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have become foundational to modern artificial intelligence. Driven by scaling laws, their rapid growth poses increasing computational and memory challenges for deployment. To accelerate the general matrix multiplication (GEMM) operations that dominate LLM computation, bit-slice architectures decompose quantized operands along the bit dimension, exposing slice-level sparsity and redundancy. However, existing bit-slice designs primarily exploit sparsity in high-order slices, while dense low-order slices still offer substantial untapped reuse opportunities. We observe that bit-slice vectors (BSVs) are highly clustered in Hamming space, with many BSVs lying only a few bit flips away from a small set of representative patterns. Based on this observation, we propose ISTS, an algorithm-hardware co-designed accelerator that leverages representative BSV patterns as shared Steiner points to reuse partial sums across slices, substantially reducing computation. Specifically, the partial sum of each target BSV can be reconstructed from that of its assigned Steiner point using only a few additions or subtractions. On the algorithmic side, we propose Steiner Absorption Table Construction (SATC), which selects a compact set of Steiner points to absorb BSVs with only a few bidirectional bit flips, while FlipPrune selectively prunes flips to further expand the reusable BSV population. On the hardware side, we design a lightweight accelerator that supports Steiner reuse for static linear layer weights and runtime-generated attention K/V tensors. Comprehensive evaluations show that ISTS achieves average speedups of $3.09\times$, $2.41\times$, $2.18\times$, $1.27\times$, and $1.41\times$ over the state-of-the-art accelerators ANT, BBS, LUT Tensor Core, Transitive Array, and MCBP-BRCR, respectively.
item.dc:creator: Yifan Wang, Zetao Guo, You Xiao, Wendi Sun, Song Chen

item.title: An Embedded Ergonomic Posture Monitoring and AI-Assisted Home Learning System on a Raspberry Pi 3B Edge Platform
item.description: arXiv:2611.34669v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: During independent home study sessions, students frequently sustain improper sitting postures, accumulate excessive sedentary hours, and experience productivity loss from off-task digital distractions. Furthermore, learners often lack real-time pedagogical scaffolding for demanding self-study curricula. To mitigate these ergonomic and instructional challenges, this paper presents an affordable, privacy-preserving cyber-physical embedded system for domestic study spaces. Engineered on a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B (1 GB RAM) paired with a UVC optical camera and a USB condenser microphone, the system executes on-device computer vision utilizing MediaPipe Pose and OpenCV to monitor upper-body alignment, sagittal head inclination, and coronal shoulder asymmetry in real time without persisting raw video streams. A deterministic finite state machine (FSM) quantifies active study durations, enforces health-compliant rest periods, and detects illicit smartphone usage. Simultaneously, an integrated multimodal AI tutoring agent parses voice and text queries via an encrypted API gateway, synthesizing Socratic conceptual hints rather than direct solutions. A lightweight parental web dashboard delivers encrypted session analytics and scheduling configurations. Empirical benchmarks on the physical prototype confirm an end-to-end inference latency of 244-250 ms at a 352x288 resolution (4.0-4.1 FPS), a trunk-angle estimation error of 4.39 degrees MAE over 5,760 synthetic ground-truth poses, a resident set size of 320 MB, a peak SoC temperature of 58.0 degrees Celsius under sustained load, and a 1.58 s total latency for the offline TTS feedback path, proving high practicality for resource-constrained edge deployment.
item.dc:creator: Truyen T. Le, Vinh Dang Ngoc, Thai Bao Huynh

item.title: Algebraic Diversity of Switching Functions
item.description: arXiv:2611.33938v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Algebraic Diversity generalizes averaging over many observations to averaging one observation over a group of transformations matched to its structure. This paper develops the framework on the Boolean cube $\mathbb{F}_2^n$ for the translations, the coordinate permutations, the hyperoctahedral group, and the general linear and affine groups. It determines the commutant of each action and gives closed forms for the group-averaged second-order statistic of one truth table, which collapses to the Walsh periodogram for the translations, to per-weight averages for the hyperoctahedral group, and to the weight up to complementation for the affine group. Bent functions are exactly those whose translation average is white, the Haar transform along an input order is the multiplexer tree of Shannon's expansion, and higher-order averages see only the weight below a first informative order, two for the translations and four for the affine group. A matched stabilizer stands in for repeated observations, since a vote over orbits of $s$ points divides by $s$ the number of noisy truth tables a target error requires. The same viewpoint gives the affine hull of a function as matched coordinates, an exact variance identity for XOR hashing, and matched hashes whose variance never exceeds that of a pairwise independent hash. Applications on public benchmarks include hash choice for approximate model counting, the decision of parity-structured formulas and the refutation of counting formulas modulo 3 and 4 from the spectra of clause blocks, separation of NPN classes by canonical spectra, tested on ISCAS-85 cut functions and all five-input classes, correction of noisy truth tables and protection of lookup tables by voting over symmetries, blind group matching, and an analog of the CLEAN algorithm that writes a truth table as the XOR of atoms in the fixed spaces of groups. All proofs are given in full.
item.dc:creator: Mitchell A. Thornton

item.title: Kolpona: An Agentic Framework with Gradient-Free Neuron Programming for RTL Generation
item.description: arXiv:2611.33973v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Open-weight large language models (LLMs) for register-transfer level (RTL) design are usually improved by fine-tuning on curated Verilog corpora, which needs large sets of verified designs and GPU training. We present Kolpona, an agentic framework that improves such models without gradient training. Its first component is neuron programming, a new form of weight-space programming (WSP) that writes single neurons in closed form into the weights to remove failure habits found on practice tasks, and keeps each edit only when testbench results on fresh tasks favour it. At inference time, tool-using agents propose designs, and a label-free selection stage delivers one design per task from the specification, the candidates and their simulations alone. On Qwen3.5-4B, edits to 16 neurons raise the VerilogEval v2 pass@1 of the model alone from 31.7% to 55.4%, and the full framework reaches 77.6%. On Qwen3.8-27B, Kolpona lifts pass@1 from 73.1% to 94.9% on VerilogEval v2 and from 66.0% to 92.0% on RTLLM v2.1 on a single 32 GB GPU, above every published system in our comparison. The RTL edits also carry over to Python and raise the pass@1 of the 4B model alone from 84.8% to 91.5% on HumanEval+ and from 67.7% to 77.5% on MBPP+.
item.dc:creator: Musa Tur Farazi, Md Nasir Uddin, Soumik Bhattacharjee, Tishna Sabrina, Chowdhury Mohammad Rakin Haider

item.title: Any-Rate: Half-Bit Multi-Precision LLM Quantization with Coded Bit-Planes
item.description: arXiv:2611.34402v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Nested multi-precision quantization derives multiple precisions from a single checkpoint by reading only the leading bits of each weight, which makes it attractive for on-device deployment under varying memory and energy budgets. However, existing methods offer only integer bits, leaving large accuracy gaps between adjacent precisions and severe degradation at 2 bits. To address this, we propose Any-Rate, which serves 2-8 bits from one checkpoint, in half-bit steps over 2-4 bits. Any-Rate restricts some bit-planes to extended Hamming codewords in 8-weight blocks (0.5 bits per weight), shares one LUT per row across precisions, and encodes all precisions jointly with a separate target for each, reducing the loss from sharing bit-planes. Across four LLMs, Any-Rate achieves state-of-the-art accuracy among multi-precision methods at 2 and 3 bits, keeping 69% of FP16 accuracy at 2 bits, and is within one point of the best at 4 bits. It decodes about as fast as existing kernels, and an LPDDR energy model estimates up to 27% less energy at equal accuracy. Code is available at https://github.com/hoonki2002/Any-Rate.
item.dc:creator: Hoonki Lee, Haechan Shin, Hyuntaek Jung, Yeonu Choi, Sangyeob Kim

item.title: DiversePlace: Diversity-Seeking Curriculum Reinforcement Learning for Macro Placement
item.description: arXiv:2611.34472v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Macro placement is a critical early-stage decision in physical design because macro locations strongly constrain subsequent implementation stages. The task is difficult because these high-impact discrete decisions must be made before downstream quality can be measured accurately, forcing training to rely on fast but imperfect training-time oracles such as half-perimeter wirelength (HPWL). Existing RL-based placers therefore mostly optimize single HPWL-driven solutions, and their long sequential horizons often require heavy search assistance or offline expert data while leaving little room to preserve multiple competitive layouts. We address this gap by making quality-controlled diversity an explicit objective for macro placement. Instead of relying on a single proxy-optimal solution, we maintain a compact archive of HPWL-competitive yet meaningfully different placements for downstream selection. We realize this idea in DiversePlace, a curriculum proximal policy optimization (PPO) framework that combines a quality-gated diversity reward with an expanding placement horizon, enabling from-scratch RL optimization while keeping exploration inside competitive HPWL regions. On the ISPD2005 benchmarks, DiversePlace consistently improves top-5, top-10, and top-20 archive diversity and achieves lower or virtually identical HPWL on all eight designs with better efficiency. Code: https://github.com/William030422/NIPS2026-DiversePlace.
item.dc:creator: Wenrui Zhou, Jiashun Liu, Wenji Fang, Zhiyao Xie, Ling Pan

item.title: High-Throughput GPU Decoding of Quantum Bivariate Bicycle Codes under Circuit-Level Noise
item.description: arXiv:2611.34481v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Bivariate bicycle (BB) codes reduce the physical-qubit overhead of quantum error correction compared to other codes such as Surface codes, but circuit-level faults create dependencies across measurement rounds that limit decoding throughput. We present a parallel-window GPU decoder that combines reusable fault patterns, compact shared-memory state, and persistent GPU workers using min-sum with Relay-BP recovery. On an RTX 5090, the proposed decoder keeps pace with one syndrome round every 1 $\mu$s across all four evaluated codes, up to [[144,12,12]] with 63-144 $\mu$s median commit delays. This rate has not been demonstrated in prior circuit-level GPU decoding studies and it provides $120\times$ higher decoding throughput than sequential sliding-window decoding. Checking neighboring detector rounds before accepting a decoding result reduces failure rates by up to 65%. For [[144,12,12]] at $p=0.002$, our proposed decoder achieves $7.58\times 10^{-6}$ failures per round, 36% lower than the published belief propagation (BP) with syndrome flipping (BP-SF) result.
item.dc:creator: Aditya Sodhani, Keshab K. Parhi

item.title: Toward Energy-Efficient and Low-Power Arrhythmia Detection for Wearable Devices
item.description: arXiv:2607.14747v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Cardiovascular diseases are the leading cause of death worldwide, and conditions such as arrhythmia often require long-term monitoring for effective detection and diagnosis. However, current wearable monitoring devices are bulky, uncomfortable, and typically rely on clinicians to manually evaluate electrocardiograms (ECGs). While Deep Learning (DL) algorithms have shown superior performance in arrhythmia detection and classification, their computational complexity coupled with high power consumption limit deployment in wearable devices. To address this challenge, this paper investigates the use of approximation techniques to reduce the power and energy consumption of DL architectures while maintaining acceptable classification performance. Specifically, techniques such as data precision reduction and approximate multiplication are investigated in a state-of-the-art DL model and its corresponding hardware architecture. The model is trained and validated using the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database, and hardware implementations employing various approximate multipliers are synthesized and evaluated. Compared with the state-of-the-art 8.75 {\mu}W (and 2.08 {\mu}J) reference architecture, our proposed architecture consumes 3.07 {\mu}W (and 2.17 {\mu}J) at 12 kHz, showing 64.9% reduction in power consumption while providing an acceptable output quality, i.e., 93.7% classification accuracy and 92.1% sensitivity. At 100 MHz, our proposed architecture consumes 9.45 mW (and 0.8 {\mu}J), showing 61.5% reduction in energy consumption as compared to the state-of-the-art architecture. These results demonstrate that our proposed approximations significantly extend wearable device battery life while preserving the required arrhythmia classification performance.
item.dc:creator: Floriaan Bulten, Yawar Rasheed, Arlene John, Vincenzo Stoico, Ghayoor Gillani

item.title: Neuromorphic architectures as numerical solvers for computational neuroscience
item.description: arXiv:2608.28387v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Neuromorphic computing is closely associated with spiking neuronal networks. However, an alternative class of so-called "rate-based" models arising from computational neuroscience and machine learning forgoes spiking interactions and instead relies on continuous coupling between neurons. Existing neuromorphic implementations designed around spike-based interactions are not well-suited for emulating such models. Here we view the distributed simulation of these models as message-passing algorithms on parallel hardware. Leveraging prior art in numerical algorithms and distributed simulation, we outline steps that enable the design of efficient digital neuromorphic accelerators for non-spiking neuronal models. In particular, we show that multi-bit packets, rather than spikes, are the most efficient communication strategy in packet-switched networks and that compared to basic numerical integration methods, higher-order differential equation solvers decrease both computation and communication costs while achieving lower numerical error, but that these benefits are ultimately limited by arithmetic precision. Using our proposed design principles, we convert an existing neuromorphic architecture into a distributed numerical solver - a spikeless neuromorphic system - for continuously-coupled neuronal models. We thereby demonstrate that our theoretical considerations indeed translate into practical advantages, namely reduced energy consumption and delay.
item.dc:creator: Jakob Jordan, Ole Richter, Congyang Li, Mihai A. Petrovici, Rajit Manohar

item.title: AgentDRC: Multi-Agent Algorithms for Spatially-Aware Automated DRC Correction
item.description: arXiv:2611.31876v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Design Rule Checking (DRC) error fixing remains a time-consuming bottleneck in physical design, often requiring manual intervention despite advanced EDA optimizations. Existing LLM-agent approaches fall short due to redundant contextual shapes, limited spatial reasoning over raw coordinates, and inefficient flat layout representations. We propose AgentDRC, which formulates iterative DRC correction as a multi-agent algorithm and introduces a spatial-aware verification and correction algorithm that reconstructs structured spatial relations among critical shapes and validates fixes through geometric and semantic constraint checking. The system coordinates four specialized agents to perceive multi-level, multi-modal geometric features, filter irrelevant shapes, and iteratively correct violations. Experiments show that AgentDRC achieves up to 30.4% pass@1 and 55.7% pass@5 on challenging violations, with 13.8% pass@5 improvement over the best baseline. We will open-source all code and benchmark tasks upon acceptance.
item.dc:creator: Pengju Liu (Katie), Nuo Xu (Katie), Winson Chen (Katie), Peijun Li (Katie), Yang (Katie), Zhao, Yu Cao, Caiwen Ding

item.title: Trading BRAM for LUTs: Hybrid Bit-Level Weight Storage for FPGA-Based Spiking Neural Networks
item.description: arXiv:2611.32288v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) offer an attractive paradigm for energy-efficient AI inference, while their deployment on reconfigurable hardware enables application-specific acceleration without sacrificing model reprogrammability. However, realizing this potential on FPGAs is often severely constrained by the immense on-chip memory needed to store synaptic weights. Existing compression techniques reduce this storage requirement at the cost of weight precision or accuracy. This work presents a hybrid bit-level weight-storage scheme that trades BRAM capacity for FPGA logic resources while preserving the original weights unmodified. Selected weight bits are implemented using Look-Up Tables (LUTs), while the remaining bits are stored in BRAM and jointly reconstructed during inference. We integrate this approach into a spatial dataflow SNN architecture and introduce a practical bit-mapping heuristic that efficiently partitions weight bits between BRAM and LUT-based logic without modifying the weights. Experimental evaluation demonstrates more than 26% reduction in BRAM utilization with a modest increase in LUT and register usage, resulting in significant overall power savings.
item.dc:creator: Dimitrios Sekertzis, Giorgos Dimitrakopoulos

item.title: Predictive Coding Implemented as a Hardware Substrate Computes Gradients faster than Backpropagation
item.description: arXiv:2603.18066v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Backpropagation has enabled modern deep learning but is difficult to realize as an online, fully distributed hardware system due to global error propagation, separate phases, and centralized memory. Predictive coding is an alternative learning algorithm with similar dynamics to backpropagation that arises from local prediction error dynamics. This paper shows that predictive coding can be instantiated as a discrete time digital hardware substrate, with local memory and computation, no instruction set architecture, and one physical core for each predictive-coding neuron. Each core stores its own activity and weights, communicates with the cores that it's connected to, and performs local gradient updates. By updating neuron cores concurrently, the architecture computes a network update in O(J+K) clock cycles. For dense layers of width n, this is O(n) cycles per update, compared with O(n^2) connection operations processed serially. This result is retained with scaling to larger predictive coding networks, demonstrating a decisive theoretical advantage for predictive coding instantiated in hardware.
item.dc:creator: Timothy Oh

item.title: SILK: Streaming Authentication with In-Place Checks for Low-bit LLM Inference
item.description: arXiv:2608.26402v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A root-of-trust (RoT) supports model authentication at load time but does not guarantee integrity during inference. We present SILK, a quantization-aware in-place integrity framework protecting low-bit large language model (LLM) weights, activations, and KV caches against runtime tampering by embedding keyed checks directly into quantized data. Weight checks are embedded during second-order post-training quantization (GPTQ) to minimize distortion, while runtime tensors use redundant codes or fallback least significant bits (LSBs). An Ascon-based authentication chain absorbs each unit's cover bits into the next unit's authentication state, enabling single-pass verification. A streaming guard permits computation after bounded-strength confirmation and holds results until full authentication. Across evaluated symmetric INT4 models, mean perplexity increases remain below 0.4% with 0.2% weight metadata. Against Dual MAC guards, SILK cuts time overhead on Qwen2.5-0.5B weight reads at 4 B/cycle from 1.95% to 0.41% (Dual MAC-256) and energy-delay product (EDP) overhead at 4-8 B/cycle by 28-69% with DDR (up to 37% with HBM2), with 28% more guard-logic area.
item.dc:creator: Ruichen Qi, Xinting Jiang, Junyi Luo, Ema Dimitrova, Quan Cheng, Mehdi Saligane
